# Learning Machines

Welcome to the interactive companion to *Learning Machines: A Statistical Introduction*. Each chapter pairs the book's exposition with code you can **run in your browser** — Python via Pyodide, R via WebR — or **open in Colab** for the deep-learning chapters. Nothing to install; the code below runs on your own machine, in this page.

::: {.howto}
[How to read this site]{.lbl}

- **Run it yourself.** Code cells run live in your browser — click **Run Code**. The Python (Pyodide) and R (WebR) runtimes start downloading as soon as a page opens, which takes a few seconds; the Run button stays grey until they are ready, then turns red. Some cells run themselves at that point and draw without a click.
- **Python or R, your choice.** Every worked example carries both. Pick a tab and the rest of the page follows; the two are genuine twins, not a translation of one into the other. (The parameter sliders and the Chapter 1 exercises are the exceptions: those controls are Python-only.)
- **Same method, sometimes different digits.** When a cell uses fixed data the two languages agree to the last digit; when a cell draws a random sample they differ a little, and that difference is the lesson — what holds is the method, not the digits.
- **The heaviest work runs in Colab.** Chapters 9–12 train in PyTorch, too heavy for a browser sandbox, so those notebooks open in Google Colab. The idea at the core of each still runs here: backpropagation from NumPy, convolution by hand, scaled dot-product attention, and a bigram language model fitted by counting.
:::

## Try it now

Here is the whole idea of Chapter 1 in six lines, and a demonstration that this page really does run code. Machine learning turns data into predictions that hold up on cases you have not seen, and before reaching for anything elaborate it pays to fix a [baseline]{.term}: the simplest model, the one that ignores every input and predicts the same number every time. For a numeric target that number is the mean. Every later chapter is a campaign to shrink the error it leaves.

Pick a tab and click **Run Code**.

## Python

```{pyodide}
import numpy as np
price = np.array([164,384,465,420,520,610,700,760,820,900,
                  560,430,500,650,720,790,980,260,330,410.])

baseline = price.mean()                       # the simplest model: predict the average
mse = ((price - baseline) ** 2).mean()        # the error it leaves behind

print(f"baseline prediction = {baseline:6.1f}")
print(f"baseline MSE        = {mse:8.1f}")
```

## R

```{webr}
price <- c(164,384,465,420,520,610,700,760,820,900,
           560,430,500,650,720,790,980,260,330,410)

baseline <- mean(price)                       # the simplest model: predict the average
mse <- mean((price - baseline)^2)             # the error it leaves behind

cat(sprintf("baseline prediction = %6.1f\n", baseline))
cat(sprintf("baseline MSE        = %8.1f\n", mse))
```

:::

The mean is the maximum-likelihood prediction under a model with no inputs. It is also, in a sense the book makes precise, where every regression starts: ordinary least squares (Chapter 2) is what you get when you let the prediction tilt with the features instead of staying flat.

## What the tilt buys

The figure above draws the flat baseline. This cell draws what happens when the prediction is allowed to follow the living area instead — and measures how much of the baseline's error that removes. It runs on its own when the page opens, so what you see below is live output; edit any number and click **Run Code** to redraw it.

::: {.panel-tabset group="lang"}

## Python

```{pyodide}
#| autorun: true
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

area = np.array([52, 82, 120, 95, 140, 160, 180, 200, 210, 225,
                 150, 110, 130, 170, 190, 205, 240, 60, 75, 100.])
price = np.array([164, 384, 465, 420, 520, 610, 700, 760, 820, 900,
                  560, 430, 500, 650, 720, 790, 980, 260, 330, 410.])

baseline = price.mean()

# the least-squares line, derived properly in Chapter 2
slope = ((area - area.mean()) * (price - price.mean())).sum() / ((area - area.mean()) ** 2).sum()
intercept = price.mean() - slope * area.mean()
fitted = intercept + slope * area

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7, 4.4))
# grey segments: the error the baseline leaves behind
for a, p in zip(area, price):
    ax.plot([a, a], [p, baseline], color="#666666", lw=0.8, alpha=0.55, zorder=1)
ax.axhline(baseline, color="#E3120B", ls="--", lw=1.6, zorder=2,
           label=f"baseline = {baseline:.0f}")
order = np.argsort(area)
ax.plot(area[order], fitted[order], color="#31417A", lw=2.2, zorder=3,
        label="least-squares line")
ax.scatter(area, price, color="#076FA1", s=44, zorder=4,
           edgecolors="white", linewidths=0.8)
ax.set_xlabel("Living area, m$^2$")
ax.set_ylabel("Price, thousand euros")
ax.set_title("One feature, live")
ax.legend(loc="upper left", frameon=False)
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()

removed = 1 - ((price - fitted) ** 2).mean() / ((price - baseline) ** 2).mean()
print(f"the line removes {removed:.1%} of the baseline's squared error")
print("that fraction has a name: it is R-squared, measured here in-sample")
```

## R

```{webr}
area <- c(52, 82, 120, 95, 140, 160, 180, 200, 210, 225,
          150, 110, 130, 170, 190, 205, 240, 60, 75, 100)
price <- c(164, 384, 465, 420, 520, 610, 700, 760, 820, 900,
           560, 430, 500, 650, 720, 790, 980, 260, 330, 410)

baseline <- mean(price)

# the least-squares line, derived properly in Chapter 2
slope <- sum((area - mean(area)) * (price - mean(price))) / sum((area - mean(area))^2)
intercept <- mean(price) - slope * mean(area)
fitted <- intercept + slope * area

plot(area, price, type = "n",
     xlab = "Living area, m^2", ylab = "Price, thousand euros",
     main = "One feature, live")
grid(col = "#e6e3da", lty = 1, lwd = 0.6)
# grey segments: the error the baseline leaves behind
segments(area, price, area, baseline, col = "#666666", lwd = 0.8)
abline(h = baseline, col = "#E3120B", lty = 2, lwd = 1.6)
abline(a = intercept, b = slope, col = "#31417A", lwd = 2.2)
points(area, price, pch = 21, bg = "#076FA1", col = "white", cex = 1.3, lwd = 0.8)
legend("topleft", c(sprintf("baseline = %.0f", baseline), "least-squares line"),
       col = c("#E3120B", "#31417A"), lty = c(2, 1), lwd = c(1.6, 2.2), bty = "n")

removed <- 1 - mean((price - fitted)^2) / mean((price - baseline)^2)
cat(sprintf("the line removes %.1f%% of the baseline's squared error\n", 100 * removed))
cat("that fraction has a name: it is R-squared, measured here in-sample\n")
```
